metadata.range: PDF pages 7-13 (printed page numbers 5-11): Week 1 preparations, Introduction to Dog Training, Basic Dog Training Theory, reinforcement, corrections.

agents.owner: The trainer/owner, addressed as 'you'. Almost every norm is written to the owner.
agents.dog: Treated as an agent. Norms on the dog (heel position, no pulling, obey despite distractions) aren't addressed to the dog in words. The owner sets them and the dog learns them through reinforcement ('enforcement_on_dog').
agents.others: Family members, the veterinarian and the public appear as secondary bearers or beneficiaries.

extraction_notes: 'text', 'conditions', 'exceptions', 'epistemic_conditions.text', 'rationale' and 'cross_refs' are verbatim from the PDF text, with three normalizations: whitespace and line breaks collapsed to single spaces, the typographic ligatures 'ﬂ'/'ﬁ' written as 'fl'/'fi', and the line-break hyphen restored in 'off-leash' (p. 9, extracted as 'offleash'). Curly quotes, en dashes and capitals are kept.
Page 9 is set in two columns. Rules 1-11 are extracted in reading order.
The sidebar on p. 12 ('Reread this paragraph…') is tagged document_part = 'sidebar'.
Purely factual sentences used as reasons are stored in 'rationale' on the norm they support, not as separate entries.
Mixed statements are split and share a 'split_group'.

label_taxonomy.Goal: Outcome to pursue, possibly with degrees of achievement.
label_taxonomy.Value: What matters, without itself fixing an action.
label_taxonomy.Disposition: A persistent orientation or character ideal rather than a single act.
label_taxonomy.Obligation: A required action or state (used when no more specific functional category fits).
label_taxonomy.Prohibition: An action or state that must not occur (used when no more specific functional category fits).
label_taxonomy.Permission: An action the system is authorized, not merely not forbidden, to take; discretionary latitude.
label_taxonomy.Default: A presumptive rule that stronger context can displace.
label_taxonomy.Definition: A statement that creates the institutional setting, roles, or concepts.
label_taxonomy.Authority: Who can create, alter, override, or delegate requirements; where authority comes from.
label_taxonomy.Priority: How multiple applicable requirements or authorities are ordered; conflict resolution.
label_taxonomy.Interpretation: How wording and intent should be read, especially under ambiguity.
label_taxonomy.Procedure: A required way to reason or decide; deliberative heuristics.
label_taxonomy.Epistemic: Requirements or facts about knowledge, truthfulness, visibility, or evidence.
label_taxonomy.Oversight: Requirements governing correction, escalation, review, shutdown, or audit.

metadata.labeling_rule: Label = the most specific functional category (Goal, Value, Disposition, Default, Definition, Authority, Priority, Interpretation, Procedure, Epistemic, Oversight). Obligation, Prohibition and Permission are used only when nothing more specific fits. The deontic status is always recorded separately in 'normative_force'. 'secondary_label' records a second category where one clearly applies.

characteristics.bearer: Who is governed (assistant, OpenAI, developer, user, platform...).
characteristics.beneficiary: Whose interests or claims it protects (users, developers, third parties, OpenAI, humanity).
characteristics.activation: conditions = verbatim triggering clauses; scope = which deployments or products it is limited to (null = everywhere).

strength.absolute: No override stated; for root-level text, can't be overridden by any message.
strength.presumptive: Holds by default/typically; yields to unstated stronger considerations.
strength.explicitly_overridable: The text names what overrides it (unless..., can be overridden by..., subject to...).
strength.implicitly_overridable: Can be displaced by contextual cues without an explicit instruction (guideline level).

temporal_structure.triggered: Activated by a condition or event.
temporal_structure.post_violation: Activated after the dog fails to comply (corrections) or after a training failure.

satisfaction.comparative: Satisfied relative to alternatives (err on the side of..., most consequential...).
satisfaction.judgment: Depends on contextual judgment (appropriate, plausible, consider...).

characteristics.epistemic_conditions: Verbatim clauses whose applicability depends on knowledge, belief, suspicion, or inference.

relations.instantiates/instantiated_by: Specific case or example of a more general norm.
relations.related: Thematic link. All relations are stored in both directions.

dog_owner_fields.bearer: Who must act or comply: owner | dog | owner and dog | family members | other family members.
dog_owner_fields.regulated_agent: Whose behaviour the norm ultimately shapes. Often differs from the bearer, e.g. a rule addressed to the owner that is really about what the dog does.

interaction.owner→dog: Owner acts on or toward the dog.
interaction.owner→self: Owner's own preparation, knowledge or conduct.
interaction.owner→third party: Involves the vet, family or public.
interaction.dog→owner: Dog's conduct relative to the owner (e.g. heel position, compliance).

dog_owner_fields.enforcement_on_dog: How the norm is enforced on the dog: positive_reinforcement | negative_reinforcement | combined | null (not dog-directed).
dog_owner_fields.epistemic_conditions.holder: Whose knowledge or perception the condition depends on: owner, dog, or 'owner (about dog)' for the owner's judgment of the dog's state.
dog_owner_fields.rationale: Verbatim reason the text gives for the norm.
dog_owner_fields.pdf_page / printed_page: PDF page index and the page number printed on the page (PDF page − 2).

metadata.rules_status: The 11 numbered items under 'Rules to train by' are introduced as 'tips', but are treated as binding rules: force and strength follow each rule's own wording, and the 'tips' framing doesn't weaken them. Hedges inside a rule ('usually' in rule 8) still make that rule presumptive.

normative_force_added.discouraged: Advised against but not forbidden ('not recommended', 'will not serve your training well'). Added for this document.

modal_marker_lists._note: Detected automatically and then corrected by hand. 'prescriptive_indicative' marks a required or prohibited norm stated in plain present tense with no modal word ('we rely exclusively on positive reinforcement', 'No corrections are given'). 'imperative' marks instructions in the imperative mood (most of this manual). can/may count as deontic only where they grant permission.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: Collar. A flat nylon or leather collar or a half-check training collar is best.
norms.label: Default
norms.context: First equipment item. A recommended default that the next sentences show can be displaced (some owners use choke chains).

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: The half-check collar is part nylon fabric and part chain link.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Defines the half-check collar.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: A choke chain is not recommended as this type of collar is implicated in doing damage to the esophagus. For this reason and because these collars have the ability to choke a dog to death, many consider them dangerous and inhumane.
norms.label: Prohibition
rationale: this type of collar is implicated in doing damage to the esophagus
these collars have the ability to choke a dog to death
norms.context: Advises against choke chains because of injury and welfare risk. 'Not recommended' rather than forbidden.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: Although people do not intend to harm their pets, these collars are very easy to misuse. Despite the drawbacks, some people will decide to use this type of collar for training.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: Acknowledges that owners keep discretion to use a choke chain despite the advice.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: If you do, it is imperative to understand how to use it properly – and for this reason, this manual includes a discussion of the correct placement and the best technique for using the choke collar (see page 25).
norms.label: Epistemic

conditions: If you do

norms.context: Knowledge requirement that applies if the owner chooses a choke chain.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: However, it bears repeating that this is a dangerous collar. It should never be left on the dog.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Absolute safety rule for choke chains.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: It should be taken off as soon as the training session is over.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: as soon as the training session is over

norms.context: Triggered by the end of a session.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: Six-foot fabric or leather leash.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Equipment item under the heading 'Get the right equipment' (imperative).

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: A chain leash is not acceptable.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Ban on chain leashes.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: Buy a leash that is flexible and you can hold easily.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Leash quality requirement.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: New leather leashes are often stiff; soften them with mineral oil.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: New leather leashes are often stiff

norms.context: Maintenance step for stiff leather leashes.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: If you have a small dog, make certain that the leash and clasp are appropriate for the dog’s size. Oversized, heavy equipment will tire out a small dog.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: If you have a small dog

rationale: Oversized, heavy equipment will tire out a small dog.
norms.context: Equipment must fit the dog's size.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: 30-foot long line. Nylon or cotton webbing or polypropylene rope with a hasp on one end. Again, make sure it is an appropriate weight for the dog.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Equipment item with a weight-appropriateness requirement.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get the right equipment
norms.text: Food tidbits. Soft food such as cubes of cheese or bits of hot dog. Toy. A ball or favourite dog toy. Fanny pack. For carrying the food tidbits.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: The remaining equipment items: these are the reinforcers used later.

norms.text: Make an appointment to see your veterinarian to make certain that your dog has no health issues that could interfere with training.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Pre-training health check by a third party (the vet).

norms.text: Deal with any problems before starting any training, and make certain your dog’s vaccinations are up to date.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Health issues must be resolved before training begins.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Get to know the characteristics of your dog’s breed
norms.text: Visit the library or browse the Internet for information about the special characteristics of your dog’s breed and how you can make use of them in training.
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: The owner should learn breed traits and use them in training.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn to hold your leash correctly
norms.text: Put your right thumb through the loop at the end of the leash. Make a single loop and hold the loop with your right hand near your waist. This frees up your left hand to pet the dog, give him treats or help position him, as necessary.
norms.label: Procedure
rationale: This frees up your left hand to pet the dog, give him treats or help position him, as necessary.
norms.context: Correct leash grip, which frees the left hand for reinforcement.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn to hold your leash correctly
norms.text: Sometimes when it’s necessary to give a collar correction, you may need to hold the leash with both hands
norms.label: Permission

conditions: when it’s necessary to give a collar correction

norms.context: Exception to the one-hand grip during a collar correction.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn to hold your leash correctly
norms.text: but as soon as the correction is completed, free up your left hand again to praise and encourage the dog.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: as soon as the correction is completed

norms.context: Return to one hand right after a correction so the owner can praise.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn the heel position
norms.text: Before practicing any heeling exercises, be certain that you completely understand the heel position.
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: The owner must understand the standard before teaching it.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn the heel position
norms.text: You and your dog are in correct heel position when the dog is no more than four inches from your left side, facing in the same direction as you.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Constitutive standard for heel position. Describes a joint state of owner and dog, but the dog is the one expected to produce it.

norms.section: Week 1 Preparations > Learn the heel position
norms.text: Whether the dog is sitting, standing, lying down or moving next to you, he is in proper heel position when the area from his head to his shoulders is in line with your left hip/leg.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: The heel standard holds in every posture.

norms.text: Before you begin the training exercises, read this introduction to dog training:
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: Owner must read the introduction before training.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: To make training a safe, productive experience for you and your dog, keep these tips in mind:
norms.label: Goal
norms.context: States the aim behind the 11 rules. The text calls them 'tips', but they are treated as binding rules here (see metadata.rules_status).

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Unless an exercise specifically requires that you take the dog off-leash, keep your dog on-leash at all times while training.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: while training

exceptions: Unless an exercise specifically requires that you take the dog off-leash
norms.context: Rule 1. On-leash by default, unless an exercise requires otherwise.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Don’t allow your dog to sniff, pester or play with other dogs before or during training sessions.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Rule 2. Rule addressed to the owner, about the dog's behavior.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Don’t feed your dog for at least four hours before training.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Rule 3. Fasting window, presumably so food works as a motivator.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Before your training practice sessions, give your dog ample opportunity to relieve himself.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Rule 4.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Take a plastic bag to practice sessions. If your dog defecates, clean it up.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: If your dog defecates

norms.context: Rule 5. A duty owed to the public or third parties.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Practise with your dog only if he is well rested.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: only if he is well rested

epistemic_conditions.text: only if he is well rested

rationale: But if your dog has played all day or has gone for a long hike, chances are that any practise sessions that day will not be effective.
norms.context: Rule 6. Training depends on the dog's physical state.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Moderate exercise a few hours before training is fine and may actually enhance learning for some high-energy dogs.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: Rule 6, permission part.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Consult this manual before practising. Read and reread instructions. Then go and practise with the dog.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Rule 7. Read first, then practise.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Remember to be patient.
norms.label: Disposition
norms.context: Rule 7. Patience as a trainer virtue.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Practise. Practise. Practise. Dogs learn by repetition. Set aside time each day to train your dog.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Rule 8. Daily practice.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: At the beginner level, a minimum of 30 minutes of practice per day is usually needed.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: At the beginner level

norms.context: Rule 8. Quantitative minimum for beginners.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: It’s always better to train for shorter periods, a couple of times a day, especially with younger or inexperienced dogs.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: especially with younger or inexperienced dogs

norms.context: Rule 8. Comparative preference for shorter, more frequent sessions.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Rough or abusive treatment will not serve your training well.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Rule 9. Treated as a binding rule like the other numbered tips: rough or abusive treatment is prohibited. The text phrases it through its ineffectiveness.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: If a dog disobeys your commands, there is a better than average chance that the problem is with you, the trainer, not the dog.
norms.label: Interpretation

conditions: If a dog disobeys your commands

epistemic_conditions.text: there is a better than average chance that the problem is with you

norms.context: Rule 9. How to read the dog's non-compliance: fault is attributed to the trainer by default.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Rethink what you’re doing, check the training manual to refresh your memory and try again.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Rule 9. The owner's remedy after the dog disobeys.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Your dog should be clean (brushed) and free of fleas.
norms.label: Obligation
rationale: Aside from being a health issue, a dog with such problems will have difficulty concentrating on the lessons and training progress will be slow.
norms.context: Rule 10. A state of the dog the owner must maintain.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: If your dog is troubled by parasites or is experiencing skin or other grooming problems, talk to your veterinarian.
norms.label: Oversight

conditions: If your dog is troubled by parasites or is experiencing skin or other grooming problems

norms.context: Rule 10. Escalation to the vet.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: If you’re training the family pet, one family member should take responsibility for training the dog and for practising the lessons each day.
norms.label: Authority

conditions: If you’re training the family pet

rationale: it’s usually easier on the dog to have the same family member act as trainer and take the dog through the course.
norms.context: Rule 11. Assigns the trainer role to a single family member.

norms.section: Introduction to Dog Training > Rules to train by
norms.text: Other family members should become familiar with commands and expectations,
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: Rule 11. Non-trainers still need to know the dog's commands, so the norms on the dog stay consistent.

norms.text: Teach each new skill or exercise to the dog in three stages:
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Introduces the three-stage method: teaching, correction, proofing.

norms.text: Teaching Stage. In this stage, the dog doesn’t understand what you’re asking of him.
norms.label: Definition

epistemic_conditions.text: the dog doesn’t understand what you’re asking of him

norms.context: The stage is defined by what the dog doesn't yet know.

norms.text: You’re now teaching the dog, using various aids, to associate a particular word or command with a desired action or behaviour. During this stage, you show the dog what you mean when you say, “Sit.” You use food and other aids to help the dog understand what you expect when you give the command.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: During this stage

norms.context: Teaching stage method: show the dog what a command means, using food and other aids.

norms.text: Correction Stage. Start correcting as soon as you feel that the dog understands your expectation.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: as soon as you feel that the dog understands your expectation

epistemic_conditions.text: as soon as you feel that the dog understands your expectation

norms.context: Moving to stage 2 depends on the owner's judgment of what the dog understands.

norms.text: Keep the food out of sight of the dog in this stage.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: in this stage

norms.context: Correction stage rule.

norms.text: If the dog responds correctly when you give the command, give him praise and a food tidbit, the motivator.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: If the dog responds correctly when you give the command

norms.context: Reward rule, triggered by the dog's compliance.

norms.text: If the dog doesn’t give the right response, correct him to get into the desired position. Once he is in the desired position give praise – and the motivator.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: If the dog doesn’t give the right response
Once he is in the desired position

norms.context: Correction then praise, triggered by the dog's non-compliance.

norms.text: Proofing Stage. This final stage starts only after the dog consistently performs the exercise correctly and no longer needs correction.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: only after the dog consistently performs the exercise correctly and no longer needs correction

norms.context: Stage 3 begins only once the dog performs reliably.

norms.text: The proofing stage seeks to ensure that the dog’s response is reliable in less-than-ideal conditions.
norms.label: Goal
norms.context: Aim of proofing: reliability.

norms.text: During this stage, you gradually introduce distractions while the dog works. If he becomes distracted, you teach him to continue to work.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: During this stage
If he becomes distracted

norms.context: Proofing method.

norms.text: Teaching him to obey despite distractions helps make him a safe dog and reliable in any situation.
norms.label: Goal
norms.context: The end-state norm for the dog: obey despite distractions. Gives the reason for proofing.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: Dog training is simply shaping the animal’s behaviour to conform to what is acceptable to people.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Constitutive statement: what is acceptable to people is the source of the norms on the dog.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: First, we need to clearly define the desired behaviour.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Step 1 of the shaping method.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: Then we break down the behaviour down into small, achievable parts. This is known as “task analysis.”
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Step 2: task analysis. (The doubled 'down' is in the original.)

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: Next, we determine what needs to be taught first. Once decided, we begin by teaching this first element and reinforcing it until the dog understands it. Then we move to the next logical element in the sequence, and so on. Each element builds on the previous element(s) until an entire behaviour is learned.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Step 3: teach elements in order, moving on only once the dog understands each one.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: There are two kinds of reinforcement: positive and negative.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Taxonomy of reinforcement.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: In the teaching stage, we rely exclusively on positive reinforcement.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: In the teaching stage

norms.context: Only positive reinforcement during teaching.

norms.section: Basic Dog Training Theory > About teaching desired behaviour
norms.text: Once we get to the correction stage of any exercise, we combine positive and negative reinforcement.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: Once we get to the correction stage of any exercise

norms.context: Both kinds of reinforcement during correction.

norms.text: A positive reinforcer is any thing or any action that the dog enjoys that, by itself, or in combination with others, will increase the likelihood that the dog will perform a desired behaviour again. Sometimes referred to as motivators, they can include food, play with a favourite toy, verbal praise, or physical stroking.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Defined by what the dog enjoys, i.e. from the dog's point of view.

norms.text: It is important that the motivator be positive to the dog.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Whether a reinforcer counts is judged from the dog's preferences.

norms.text: If, for example, you were training a dog that doesn’t like to be stroked (yes, there are some) then petting the dog when he has performed a desired behaviour would actually work against your training.
norms.label: Interpretation
norms.context: Example: stroking stops being a reinforcer for a dog that dislikes it.

norms.text: When the dog gives you a desired behaviour, particularly in the early stages of teaching a specific exercise, positive reinforcement should have the following component parts:
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: When the dog gives you a desired behaviour
particularly in the early stages of teaching a specific exercise

norms.context: Lead-in to the three components of positive reinforcement.

norms.text: Verbal praise. Make it genuine and enthusiastic.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Component 1. Also sets the manner: genuine and enthusiastic.

norms.text: Stroking or petting the dog – if the dog enjoys it.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: if the dog enjoys it

norms.context: Component 2, conditional on the dog's preference.

norms.text: Food tidbit or play with a favourite toy or ball.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Component 3.

norms.text: Negative reinforcement is an action or stimulus that the dog interprets as negative, which by itself or in combination with other reinforcers will increase the likelihood that the dog will perform a desired behaviour again, or will reduce the likelihood that he will perform an unwanted behaviour again.
norms.label: Definition

epistemic_conditions.text: that the dog interprets as negative

norms.context: Also defined by how the dog interprets it.

norms.text: Select a negative reinforcer that will manipulate the dog into correcting an unwanted behaviour by substituting it with a wanted or desired behaviour.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: A negative reinforcer must steer the dog toward a replacement behaviour.

norms.text: If your dog is pulling on the leash, you quickly step to the side and pop the leash and collar so that you slightly off-balance him. To avoid the discomfort, the dog stops pulling on the leash and instead, walks with a loose leash.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: If your dog is pulling on the leash

norms.context: Worked example of negative reinforcement for leash pulling.

norms.text: Note that the dog has control over this situation. He can avoid the discomfort merely by correcting his actions, in this case, by walking at your left side and letting the leash go slack.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: The dog's agency: it always has a way to end the aversive stimulus by complying. This is what separates negative reinforcement from punishment.

norms.section: No place for punishment in dog training
norms.text: The term negative reinforcement is often used interchangeably with the word “punishment.” IN DOG TRAINING, THEY’RE NOT THE SAME THING.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Conceptual distinction, emphasized in capitals in the original.

norms.section: No place for punishment in dog training
norms.text: Punishment: Is usually dished out after the fact. Usually has a negative emotional component, carrying with it frustration or anger. Usually fails to give the dog a way out. He cannot correct a behaviour in order to stop the discomfort.
norms.label: Definition
norms.context: Three typical features of punishment: delayed, emotional, and leaving the dog no way out.

norms.section: No place for punishment in dog training
norms.text: Punishment neither increases desired behaviour nor decreases undesirable behaviour. It’s useless as a training tool and has no place in dog training.
norms.label: Prohibition
rationale: Punishment neither increases desired behaviour nor decreases undesirable behaviour.
norms.context: Categorical ban on punishment, justified by its ineffectiveness.

norms.text: Combining negative reinforcement with positive reinforcement starts in the correction stage of an exercise.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: When combined reinforcement begins.

norms.text: Say your dog is tugging on the leash. You say, “No pulling” and quickly step to the right and pop the collar to slightly off-balance the dog. The pop on the collar is negative reinforcement. To avoid the negative sensation, the dog backs off and stops pulling on the leash. You instantly say, “Good no pulling!” in an excited and obviously pleased voice. That’s positive reinforcement.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Worked example: name the behaviour, correct it, then praise immediately.

norms.text: This combining of reinforcers is your most powerful teaching tool and the dog’s best opportunity to learn. Combining reinforcers sidesteps punishment by giving the dog an acceptable, alternative behaviour and helps name that behaviour: “No pulling.”
norms.label: Value
norms.context: Rates combined reinforcement as the best tool and contrasts it with punishment.

norms.text: If you apply the correction effectively each time the dog pulls the leash tight, he’ll learn not only that pulling is unacceptable, but also what the words “no pulling” mean.
norms.label: Prohibition

conditions: If you apply the correction effectively each time the dog pulls the leash tight

epistemic_conditions.text: he’ll learn not only that pulling is unacceptable

norms.context: A norm on the dog ('pulling is unacceptable'), which the dog comes to know through consistent correction by the owner.

norms.text: Once this happens, you can start to substitute a voice correction for a jerk or tug on the leash.
norms.label: Permission

conditions: Once this happens

norms.context: Unlocked once the dog has learned the cue: switch from physical to voice correction.

norms.text: In the teaching stage, you offer positive reinforcement each and every time you ask for, and get, a desired behaviour.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: In the teaching stage

norms.context: Positive reinforcement on every success during teaching.

norms.text: No corrections are given.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: No corrections during teaching.

norms.text: Reread this paragraph. It is key to successful training.
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: Sidebar callout marking the teaching-stage rule as essential.

norms.text: Once we move to the correction stage, we correct undesirable behaviour.
norms.label: Procedure

conditions: Once we move to the correction stage

norms.context: Correcting begins in the correction stage.

norms.text: Every time you correct a dog for undesirable behaviour (negative reinforcer), you must praise him (positive reinforcer) when he corrects the behaviour.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: when he corrects the behaviour

norms.context: Every correction must be followed by praise once the dog complies.

norms.text: If the correction is hard, then you must praise him with equal energy when he corrects that behaviour. This is extremely important.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: If the correction is hard

norms.context: Proportionality: praise must match the strength of the correction.

norms.text: When trainers overuse negative reinforcement and/or don’t balance it with equal or better positive reinforcement, their dogs begin to lose their will to try. Their enthusiasm wanes. They try to avoid the trainer; they hate the work and they look as if they have been abused.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Implicit ban on overusing correction, stated through its effects on the dog's motivation and welfare.

norms.text: The positive reinforcer you choose will depend on the exercise you’re teaching. Certain exercises lend themselves to food tidbits while others lend themselves better to voice praise or physical stroking. A certain amount of discretion is needed here.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: Owner's discretion in choosing reinforcers.

norms.text: For young dogs, food tidbits are very motivating and using them will speed up learning.
norms.label: Default

conditions: For young dogs

norms.context: Food as the default reinforcer for young dogs.

norms.text: Eventually, we will want to wean ourselves, and the dog, from using food so that the dog works primarily for praise.
norms.label: Goal
norms.context: Long-term goal: the dog works for praise rather than food.

norms.text: To get ready for this, you must always PRAISE and/or STROKE the dog as you reward him with a food tidbit.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: as you reward him with a food tidbit

norms.context: Pair praise with food so praise can take over later. (Capitals are in the original.)

norms.text: If you start training your dog using food, you must systematically and slowly withdraw food as the primary reinforcer.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: If you start training your dog using food

norms.context: Gradual food withdrawal.

norms.text: You can still use food occasionally to reward a job well done. In fact, occasionally rewarding the dog with a motivator in addition to praise is good practice.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: Occasional food rewards stay permitted, even recommended.

norms.text: However, eventually verbal and physical praise need to become the primary reinforcers. Food needs to become a secondary or even a tertiary reinforcer.
norms.label: Priority
rationale: If you have paired the positive reinforcers, verbal and physical praise will take on more importance than food tidbits to most dogs.
norms.context: Final ranking of reinforcers.

norms.text: The choice of negative reinforcers should be based on the option which is the least intrusive to get the job done.
norms.label: Procedure
norms.context: Least-intrusive-means principle for corrections.

norms.text: For example, voice correction is less intrusive than a collar correction. If a voice correction will get the desired results, there is no need to apply the stronger correction.
norms.label: Priority

conditions: If a voice correction will get the desired results

epistemic_conditions.text: If a voice correction will get the desired results

norms.context: Ranks voice correction below collar correction in intrusiveness.

norms.text: An important part of the art of dog training lies in which corrections you choose and how you give them. As training progresses, you’ll develop an intuitive sense about the level and type of correction your dog needs.
norms.label: Disposition
norms.context: The trainer's skill develops into intuition over time.

norms.text: Some dogs are very sensitive. Slight pressure on the collar will produce the desired, or corrected, behaviour. Others may need a stronger pop on the collar. Situations also vary. In some cases, a voice correction will get the desired result. Others will call for a collar correction.
norms.label: Epistemic
norms.context: Correction strength has to be calibrated to the individual dog and the situation.

norms.text: You need to apply corrections swiftly and give them where the dog is.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Corrections must be immediate and given close to the dog.

norms.text: Trying to influence a dog’s behaviour from a distance generally relies on voice commands. At the beginner level of training, such attempts are useless for two reasons: The dog lacks the experience for voice corrections to be effective. As a trainer, you have no back-up plan if the voice correction fails. You have no way to follow through with the dog to make sure he obeys you and corrects the behaviour.
norms.label: Prohibition

conditions: At the beginner level of training

epistemic_conditions.text: The dog lacks the experience for voice corrections to be effective

rationale: Relying on voice correction at this early stage will most likely lead you into the trap of unwittingly training your dog to not respond to you.
norms.context: Advises against correcting from a distance at the beginner level. The reason is enforceability: the owner can't follow through.

norms.text: At all times you should also give corrections with a matter-of-fact style. It’s a straightforward process and a correction is nothing more and nothing less than a training tool.
norms.label: Obligation
norms.context: Manner of correcting: calm and impersonal.

norms.text: Very simply, your dog didn’t comply with your command, so you prompt or position him until he produces the desired behaviour.
norms.label: Definition

conditions: your dog didn’t comply with your command

norms.context: Defines a correction functionally.

norms.text: Take care to never charge your corrections with emotion. Anger and frustration have no place in dog training.
norms.label: Prohibition
norms.context: Absolute ban on emotional corrections.

norms.text: Your own emotions should enter the picture only as part of the positive reinforcement – the praise.
norms.label: Permission
norms.context: Restricted permission: emotion is allowed only in praise.

norms.text: When your dog behaves correctly, praise him lavishly – and with genuine feeling.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: When your dog behaves correctly

norms.context: Manner of praise.

norms.text: You must praise after each correction as soon as the dog complies and you must make the praise at least as strong as the correction.
norms.label: Obligation

conditions: as soon as the dog complies

norms.context: Restates the proportionality rule with an immediacy requirement.
